source.title: Beyond Owls: Subliminal Learning Can Transfer Learned Capabilities and Backdoors
source.authors: Jan Dubinski; Anna Sztyber-Betley; Jan Betley; Owain Evans

page_placements.theme: Capability transfer through semantically unrelated outputs

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends subliminal learning to new traits and settings—capabilities, a conditional backdoor, and hacking—using teacher-generated, semantically unrelated training data.
record.gate_note: The study reports outcomes from filtered-data student training and tests a different-base student, so these are included. It also reports system-prompt experiments, but those do not test the prompt-only linked-token analogue in version F. Teacher performance created by deliberate finetuning or steering is not counted as evidence of spontaneous behavior. Results cited from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: Same-base students fine-tuned on filtered, task-unrelated teacher outputs (word continuations, Alpaca answers, number sequences) are measured for new traits. These traits are a random-MLP capability, letter counting, a French-on-female-name backdoor, and chess hacking, each against base and control students. The study also tests a different-base student (B), LoRA configurations and held-out evaluations (E). It compares students with directly optimised single-layer steering vectors, which bears on the steering-vector account in D.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors add that on the random-MLP and letter-counting tasks, subliminal learning beats system prompting and, out of distribution, single-layer steering. They read their results as consistent with steering-vector distillation explaining some transfer, but not all.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the same-base teacher/student and unrelated-data fine-tuning pattern, but tests new traits and varies the recipe. Several experiments use filtered top-32 logit distillation rather than sampled tokens; LoRA rank and target layers also vary.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer varies with logit distillation versus sampled tokens, LoRA target layers and rank, the random MLP initialization, and the tested evaluation condition. The paper reports stronger letter-counting transfer with attention-only LoRA and weaker backdoor transfer with all-module configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: No tested system prompt reproduces the transferred capabilities. The best letter-counting prompt reaches 29.8% against 44.1% for the student. Every random-MLP prompt is worse than the mean predictor (MAE ≥5.59 versus 5.46).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminally transferred capabilities can exceed what system prompting elicits from the base model.

record.problems: The authors describe their results as an existence proof and say they do not establish general rules or production relevance. Random-MLP results vary across target-network initializations. Backdoor results vary across seeds and LoRA configurations. Hacking estimates use 64 episodes per run and are described as noisy. No full-fine-tuning result is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant measured results were omitted. System-prompt performance results were left out because they do not test the linked-token prompt-only analogue in version F; teacher performance produced by deliberate finetuning or steering was also excluded as evidence of spontaneous behavior.

untested.parts: Code and maths-reasoning transfer data. Animal-preference traits.
Cross-base pairs other than Qwen3.6 to Nemotron. Traits other than letter counting.
Broad emergent misalignment, scheming and secret loyalties. Only a backdoor proxy and narrow chess hacking are tested.
Token entanglement, divergence tokens and gradient arguments. Whether students' activations align with a steering direction.
All of it: no linked-token prompting without fine-tuning.

missing.what: The hacking students' mean win rate is 43.2%, against 90.6% for the teacher. Base and control win rates are 7.8%, 1.6% and 6.2%.
Sampled-token random-MLP student: MAE 5.88, with 100% valid four-integer format against 0.1% for the base model. This is format transfer without capability transfer.
Rank-1 LoRA backdoor runs across hyperparameters all show a margin-gap shift, some without any French completions. Transfer speed varies substantially.
Per-seed student margin gaps of +10.0, +10.5 and +15.6 nats, against teacher gaps of +35.3 to +49.5.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's B label was inverted. B predicts no cross-base transfer, so R8 supports it. Steering-vector rows (R26, R27, R29) measure the comparator, not the student, so their E links were removed. Teachers are built by deliberate fine-tuning or steering, as subliminal learning requires; only the students' behaviour counts. Several results use top-32 logit distillation and attention-only LoRA, which differ from the original recipe; the authors note this. The study is co-authored by original-source authors but is not itself an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test every possible unrelated output type; its main settings are word continuations, Alpaca answers, and number sequences.
Cross-base transfer is tested for letter counting only, using a Qwen teacher and Nemotron student.
The study tests a French-trigger backdoor and a narrow chess-hacking propensity, not other forms of misalignment such as scheming or secret loyalties.

The study tests whether a directly optimized, single-layer steering vector reproduces two capabilities. It does not test token entanglement, divergence tokens, or a gradient-based explanation of the subliminal signal.
It tests selected LoRA configurations and held-out evaluation conditions. It does not test full fine-tuning.
No experiment inserts linked tokens into prompts without fine-tuning.

relationships.condition: Same-base Qwen students: letter counting with attention-only LoRA, logit-distilled backdoor, logit-distilled hacking, and the strongest random-MLP network
relationships.reason: The students show clear trait gains over controls on unrelated data. Letter counting reaches 59.8% against a 26.6% control (R7, R6). The backdoor gives 23.5% French against 0% (R9). Hacking rises to 58.3% against at most 7.3% for controls (R19–R22, R23, R24). The strongest MLP student reaches R2 0.38 (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Students beat controls on unrelated data: letter counting reached 59.8% vs 26.6%, the backdoor produced 23.5% French vs 0%, and hacking rose to 58.3% vs at most 7.3%. The strongest MLP student reached an R² of 0.38.
